title: The Hiphil and the Hophal

objectives.can: Recognise and parse Hiphil and Hophal forms.

explanation.summary: The Hiphil is the third commonest stem. It is marked by a he at the front of the qatal, the imperative and the infinitive, by an a-vowel under the yiqtol prefix, and by a long i before the last root consonant in most third person forms. The Hophal is its passive. The Hiphil is often causative, but not always.

sections.heading: The shape of the Hiphil
body: In the qatal the Hiphil begins with a prefixed he and an i-vowel: הִבְדִּיל. Before a consonantal ending the long i is replaced by a short a: הִבְדַּלְתִּי, 'I separated'. The yiqtol has an a-vowel under the person prefix and keeps the long i: יַבְדִּיל. The participle has a prefixed mem with an a-vowel: מַבְדִּיל. The infinitive construct has the prefix he with an a-vowel and the long i: לְהַבְדִּיל; the infinitive absolute has a ṣere: הַבְדֵּל. The imperative has a prefixed he with an a-vowel and a ṣere: הַקְהֶל in Deuteronomy 4:10.
The Hiphil is easy to tell from the Qal in the yiqtol: the Qal prefix has an i-vowel (יִשְׁמֹר) and the Hiphil an a-vowel (יַבְדִּיל). In the qatal, the prefixed he does the work.

sections.heading: Shortened forms
body: In the strong verb the long i of the third person is often replaced by a ṣere in the wayyiqtol and the jussive: וַיַּבְדֵּל in Genesis 1:4 beside the yiqtol יַבְדִּיל. You met the shortened forms of the wayyiqtol in the Qal; the Hiphil shows them very clearly. In the first person both shapes occur: וָאַבְדִּל and וָאַבְדִּילָה are both wayyiqtols of the same verb.
A shortened form does not change the meaning. It is a mark of the wayyiqtol or the jussive, as the form of the Qal wayyiqtol is.

sections.heading: The Hophal
body: The Hophal is the passive partner of the Hiphil. It has a prefixed he with an o-vowel (a qamets-hatuf) or a u-vowel, a shewa under the first root consonant and an a-vowel after it: הָפְקַד in Leviticus 5:23, 'was deposited'. In the yiqtol the prefix vowel is u or o: וַיֻּגַּד and יוּמַת. In roots with a weak middle consonant the u is written with a vav: הוּמָת, 'was put to death'.

The Hophal is rare: about four hundred forms in the Bible against more than nine thousand in the Hiphil. It often has the sense of the Hiphil's passive: the Hiphil הִגִּיד means 'told' and the Hophal וַיֻּגַּד means 'it was told' in 1 Samuel 15:12. The participle is analysed in the library's edition as a 'passive participle': הַמּוּמָתִים, 'those put to death'.

sections.heading: What the Hiphil does to the sense
body: The Hiphil is often causative: it adds someone who makes the action happen. The Hiphil הוֹצִיא is 'bring out' beside the Qal 'go out'; הֵבִיא is 'bring', beside 'come'; הֶעֱלָה is 'bring up', beside 'go up'; הוֹדִיעַ is 'make known', beside 'know'. With a verb of state the Hiphil often means 'make so': the Qal of the root of הֶחֱזִיק is 'be strong', and the Hiphil is 'make strong' or 'seize'.

Sometimes the Hiphil is declarative: it states that a person is something. In Deuteronomy 25:1 the judges 'justify the righteous' and 'condemn the wicked', that is, they declare the one righteous and the other guilty. And sometimes the Hiphil is neither: וַיַּשְׁכֵּם, 'he rose early', in 1 Samuel 15:12 is simply the verb's idiom, and the English of 'make' has nothing to do with it.

The Piel and the Hiphil can both sometimes be glossed with 'make', but they differ. The Piel factitive tends to go with roots that name a state ('make great'); the Hiphil causative tends to go with roots that name an action. Each root has its own record, and the lexicon is the guide.

sections.heading: Reading the Hiphil and the Hophal
body: Find the prefix: a he at the front of a qatal, imperative or infinitive; a mem with an a-vowel in the participle; an a-vowel under the person letter in the yiqtol. Then see whether the vowel after the prefix he is an i (Hiphil) or an o or a u (Hophal). In the third person look for the long i before the last root consonant, and remember that the wayyiqtol and the jussive may show a ṣere in its place.

misunderstandings: The Hiphil is not always causative. It can be declarative, can be the ordinary form of a verb, and in a few verbs has a meaning that is not 'cause' at all.
The Hophal is not the passive of the Qal. Passives of the Qal are usually Niphals; the Hophal is the passive of the Hiphil.
A shortened Hiphil is not a different stem. The ṣere of וַיַּבְדֵּל and the long i of יַבְדִּיל belong to the same stem.
A prefixed he does not always mean a Hiphil or a Hophal. It can also be the article or a question particle, and the Hiphil's he is absent from the yiqtol and the participle.

deeper.heading: Hiphil and Aramaic
body: Aramaic has a causative stem of the same kind, with a prefixed aleph or he. Some books of the Bible contain Aramaic, and you will meet the Aramaic causative there. Within Hebrew, the Hiphil and the Hophal form a pair of the same kind as the Piel and the Pual.

quoted.english: And God saw the light, that it was good; and God divided the light from the darkness.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: וַיַּרְא is a Qal wayyiqtol: God saw. וַיַּבְדֵּל is a Hiphil wayyiqtol, third masculine singular, of the root 'be separate': God separated the light from the darkness. The ṣere is the shortened form of the long i of the yiqtol. The Hiphil adds an agent who makes the separation.

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: And Samuel rose early to meet Saul in the morning; and it was told Samuel, saying: 'Saul came to Carmel, and, behold, he is setting him up a monument, and is gone about, and passed on, and gone down to Gilgal.'

examples.analysis: Three forms in one verse. וַיַּשְׁכֵּם is a Hiphil wayyiqtol, 'he rose early', a verb whose Hiphil is idiomatic, not causative. וַיֻּגַּד is a Hophal wayyiqtol: 'it was told', the passive of the Hiphil of the verb 'tell'. מַצִּיב is a Hiphil participle with the prefix mem and an a-vowel: 'setting up'.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth My people the children of Israel out of Egypt.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: וְהוֹצֵא is a Hiphil imperative, second masculine singular: 'bring out'. The prefixed he has become hô because the first root consonant is yod, a weak consonant (this is explained in the unit on weak roots). The verb is causative: Moses is to cause the people to go out. The next verse has the yiqtol form of the same verb.

examples.analysis: מוֹת is a Qal infinitive absolute, and יוּמָת is a Hophal yiqtol, third masculine singular: 'he will be put to death'. The u-vowel under the prefix marks the Hophal. The stem is the passive of the Hiphil of the same root, and the infinitive absolute before it gives emphasis.
